title: Is aphantasia a separate group or the low end of a continuum? A taxometric analysis of visual and multisensory imagery
description: Researchers disagree about whether aphantasia is a separate group of people or the low end of a continuum of imagery vividness, and cut-offs on the VVIQ cannot settle this. We use taxometric analysis, which was built for this question, on VVIQ answers from 35,467 people collected by the Aphantasia Network (Monzel et al., 2026). Because that website sample over-represents weak imagery, we also analyse a subsample matched to an unselected population, run a simulated continuum with the same floor, and test an unselected sample (Dance et al., 2022) and eight-sense imagery data (New et al., 2026). We ask whether low imagery is a separate group, and if so how large it is.

responses.72-2:
People with aphantasia report little or no visual imagery. Researchers disagree about what kind of difference this is. One view treats aphantasia as a condition: a separate group of people who differ in kind from everyone else. The other treats it as the low end of a continuum of imagery vividness, so any cut-off is a convention (Blomkvist and Marks, 2023). Monzel et al. (2026) compared five ways of defining aphantasia from Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ) answers in 35,467 people. Cut-offs and cluster analyses cannot show whether such groups are real, because both produce groups whatever the underlying structure is.

Taxometric analysis was built for this question. In this plan, a taxon means a separate group of people who differ in kind from everyone else. The analysis asks whether the way several measures of the same thing relate to each other looks more like data from a taxon plus everyone else, or from one continuum. A meta-analysis of 183 taxometric studies found most psychological differences are continuous, with a few possible exceptions, including autism (Haslam et al., 2020). We found no taxometric study of aphantasia.

1. Is low visual imagery, as measured by the VVIQ, a taxon or a continuum?
2. If it is a taxon, how large is it?
3. Is low imagery across several senses a taxon or a continuum?
responses.72-4:
We test two competing descriptions and make no prediction about which will fit better.
Taxon: the data fit simulated taxon data better than simulated continuous data.
Continuum: the data fit simulated continuous data better.

The main question is question 1, in the main sample (the Aphantasia Network data). Questions 2 and 3 are secondary.

responses.72-20: We collected no new data. The Aphantasia Network ran the VVIQ on its public website, so people with weak imagery are heavily over-represented, as Monzel et al. note. Dance et al. tested students and Mechanical Turk workers who were not recruited for their imagery. New et al. ran two online surveys of adults recruited through Prolific, with attention checks.
responses.72-24:
VVIQ (main and Dance et al. samples): 16 items answered from 1 (no image at all) to 5 (perfectly clear and as vivid as normal vision); total 16 to 80. The items form four scenes of four items: a relative or friend (1-4), a rising sun (5-8), a shop (9-12), a country scene (13-16). Main sample columns VVIQ_01 to VVIQ_16 and subject_id; Dance et al. columns vviq_1 to vviq_16.

New et al.: each sense score is the sum of five 1-7 ratings (5 to 35). We use the eight senses measured in both surveys: image (sight), sound, touch, motor (movement), taste, smell, emotion and voice. nbact is the number of attention checks passed.
responses.72-29: None. This is an observational secondary analysis of existing data.
responses.72-33:
Indicators, all reversed so that higher means weaker imagery:
- VVIQ samples: the four scene sums (4 to 20 each). Robustness: eight item pairs (1-2, 3-4, and so on).
- Multisensory sample: the eight sense scores, as z-scores within each survey.

Provisional taxon share (the share of people with the highest summed indicator scores put in the provisional taxon): the share with a VVIQ total of 32 or below in the VVIQ samples; the share with at least four of the eight senses at the lowest possible score in the multisensory sample.
responses.72-35: People with any missing item are left out. No values are filled in.
responses.72-39: We remove no outliers. In the main sample, repeat entries with the same subject_id are removed (the first is kept). In New et al.'s surveys we keep people who passed at least 3 attention checks, as New et al. did. The code stops if an answer is outside the questionnaire's range, a needed column is missing, or a data file does not match its SHA-256.
responses.72-41: No weights. To check whether the website sample's over-representation of weak imagery drives the result, we draw a population-matched subsample of the main sample: VVIQ totals are split into 16 bands of 4 points, and people are sampled at random without replacement from each band so the band proportions match the pooled Dance et al. data (largest possible subsample, seed 20261011).
responses.72-44: Monzel et al. (2026) report how many people fall below five VVIQ-based definitions of aphantasia and that the VVIQ items behave as a single scale. Dance et al. (2022) report the prevalence of aphantasia in their samples. New et al. (2026) report how imagery varies across senses. None of them ran a taxometric analysis.
responses.72-46:
Main sample: we have read Monzel et al. (2026). We have looked at the file's column names and number of rows, and nothing else.
Dance et al. sample: we have looked at the column names, the number of rows and the readme.
Multisensory sample: we have used New et al.'s data in earlier work, including how often people score at the lowest possible level in each sense, and how imagery differs between people who did or did not report autism or ADHD (a separate preregistered study, https://osf.io/87udm). We have not run any taxometric or mixture analysis on it.
The analysis code will not run until this plan is registered. Its tests use only simulated data.
responses.72-49:
All analyses use R with the RTaxometrics package (version 3.2.1) with default settings (100,000-case comparison populations, 100 comparison samples of each kind), seed 20261011.

For each analysis we run three procedures:
- MAMBAC sorts people on one indicator and compares the average of another indicator above and below many cut points. With a taxon the difference peaks near the best cut; with a continuum it is highest at the ends.
- MAXEIG sorts people on one indicator and, in overlapping slices, measures how strongly the other indicators go together. With a taxon this peaks where the groups mix.
- L-Mode looks at the distribution of scores on what the indicators share. A taxon tends to give two peaks.

The package compares the real curves with curves from 100 simulated taxon data sets and 100 simulated continuous data sets that copy the real indicators' distributions and correlations. The result is the comparison curve fit index (CCFI, 0 to 1; higher means more taxon-like), averaged across the three procedures (Ruscio et al., 2018).

We also run a CCFI profile: the comparison repeated at 39 taxon sizes from 2.5% to 97.5%. It gives a summary CCFI (weighted towards the best-fitting sizes) and an estimated taxon size. In samples over 5,000 the profile uses a random subsample of 5,000.

Full plan: preregistration.md at https://github.com/i-habib/aphantasia (SHA-256 23a4b7511953c929bbdb03b9e1b27e4a528e71a521e35938ae31d12e8a5d53bc); code scripts/p8_taxometrics.R.
responses.72-51: The CCFI for each procedure and their average; the CCFI profile's summary CCFI and estimated taxon size. If low imagery looks like a taxon, its size is compared with the shares at or below VVIQ 32 and 23.
responses.72-53: The samples are fixed. Taxometric analysis works best with at least 300 people and a taxon of at least about 10% of the sample. The main sample is very large and has many people with weak imagery. The population-matched subsample, the Dance et al. sample and the multisensory sample will have far fewer such people, so we expect less clear results there.
responses.72-55:
One analysis: an average CCFI of 0.55 or above reads as taxon, 0.45 or below as continuum, and anything between as unclear.

The main analysis reads as taxon only if both the main CCFI and the profile's summary CCFI read as taxon, and as continuum only if both read as continuum. Otherwise it is unclear.

Conclusion for question 1, rules applied in order:
1. Main reads as taxon, and a simulated continuum with the same floor also reads as taxon: we cannot tell a taxon from a floor effect.
2. Main reads as taxon, but the two random halves do not both read as taxon: unclear.
3. Main reads as taxon, the population-matched subsample reads as continuum, and the detectability check detects its simulated taxon: a taxon may exist, but the result could come from how the website sample was collected.
4. Main reads as taxon and none of the above applies: low visual imagery looks like a taxon.
5. Main reads as continuum: the VVIQ data give no support for a boundary between people with and without aphantasia.
6. Main unclear: the data cannot tell the two apart.

We also report, without changing the conclusion, whether the three procedures point in opposite directions, whether the result is lower-trust, and how the other robustness checks compare. Question 2 uses the CCFI profile's size estimate. Question 3 and the Dance et al. sample are read with the one-analysis rule, giving an unclear result little weight because the provisional taxa there are small.
responses.72-57:
Data checks for every analysis: how well each indicator separates the provisional taxon from everyone else (Cohen's d; 1.25 or more is the usual guide) and full tables of correlations within each group (0.30 or less is the usual guide). We run every analysis whatever these show, but call the result lower-trust if most indicators separate the groups by less than d = 1.25, or if the average within-group correlation in either group is above 0.30. We expect high within-group correlations because the scene scores are parts of one questionnaire.

If a provisional taxon would hold fewer than 30 people, that analysis is not run and is reported as not possible. When the cut for the provisional taxon falls inside a block of identical scores, the package moves the whole block to one side; we report the share actually used.
responses.72-59:
In the main sample:
1. Population-matched subsample, with its own provisional taxon share and CCFI profile. This check can only weaken a taxon result.
2. Eight item-pair indicators instead of four scene scores.
3. Provisional taxon share set to the share at or below 23, and, if the profile reads as taxon, to the profile's estimated size.
4. Two random halves (seed 20261011), each with its own share at or below 32.
5. A wider unclear zone, 0.40 to 0.60, for the main analysis only.

Simulation checks, run through the same steps:
- Floor check: a simulated continuum with the same floor (one normal underlying factor; each item cut so its answer proportions match the real item; factor strength set so the simulated items correlate as strongly on average as the real ones; same n as the main sample).
- Detectability check: a simulated known taxon with the matched subsample's size, taxon share, indicator separation and within-group correlations, to show whether the matched check could detect a taxon at all.

Secondary samples: the same analysis in the Dance et al. sample and the multisensory sample.
responses.72-61: None planned beyond the analyses above. Anything else will be reported as exploratory.
